notes.meaning: The Lord introduces a weighty message concerning Israel by reminding everyone who He is. He spread out the heavens, laid the earth's foundations, and formed the inner spirit of every human being. Because He made everything from scratch, He has total power to carry out whatever He promises to do.

The Lord warns that attacking Jerusalem will be like drinking a cup of intoxicating wine that makes the surrounding nations stumble and fall. Both the countryside of Judah and the city of Jerusalem will face a siege. Yet the very nations that try to swallow the city will end up reeling in ruin under God's judgment.

Jerusalem is compared to a massive, immovable boulder that all the nations try to haul away. Young men often tested their strength by lifting heavy rocks, but attempting to lift this stone causes severe wounds. Any world power that tries to crush God's city will only tear itself to pieces in the attempt.

The Lord promises to throw the enemy's warhorses and riders into total panic, confusion, and blindness. Warhorses represented the greatest military strength of the ancient world. God turns old covenant curses against Israel's attackers while keeping a tender, watchful eye on Judah to protect them.

The regional leaders of Judah will realize in their hearts that Jerusalem's citizens are their true strength. They know this strength does not come from human walls, but from the Lord of Hosts who defends them. Seeing God deliver the capital gives the rest of the land deep courage to trust Him.

The Lord will make Judah's leaders like a blazing pot of coals among firewood, or a torch dropped into dry sheaves of wheat. They will quickly burn up the enemy armies surrounding them on every side. Through God's power, Jerusalem will stay safe and firmly rooted in her own place.

The Lord chooses to rescue the unprotected tents of the rural countryside before He saves Jerusalem. Country people lived in open fields without high stone walls and were far more vulnerable to attack. God saves them first so the royal house of David and the proud city dwellers cannot boast that their own status saved the nation.

The Lord will shield Jerusalem so powerfully that even the weakest person who stumbles will fight with the bravery of King David. The royal house of David will lead them like God Himself, marching ahead like the angel of the Lord in the wilderness. God delights in filling the frailest believers with His own strength to overcome great trials.

The Lord sets His firm purpose to destroy every hostile nation that marches against Jerusalem. His rescue will not be partial or temporary. He will completely break the power of every empire that tries to wipe out His people.

The Lord promises to pour out the Holy Spirit to give His people a heart of grace and prayer. They will look in faith upon the One they pierced, realizing the horror of what has been done. Their grief will be as deep and heartbreaking as parents weeping for their only child or a firstborn son.

differ.view: This promise looks forward to the end times, when the Jewish nation will see the returning Christ, repent, and be saved as a whole.
This began at Pentecost and continues throughout the church age whenever the Holy Spirit leads sinners to repent before the cross of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note ancient Greek translations read 'because they mocked me,' which they take as an allusion to a rejected prophet rather than a pierced Messiah.

notes.meaning: The grief in Jerusalem will be as overwhelming as the famous national mourning at Hadad-rimmon in the valley of Megiddo. That valley was where good King Josiah was mortally wounded, plunging the whole kingdom into deep sorrow. The future repentance of God's people will be just as widespread, sincere, and heartbreaking.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Hadad-rimmon refers to ritual weeping for ancient pagan storm and thunder gods in fertility cults rather than the death of King Josiah.

notes.meaning: The entire land will mourn family by family in private, including the royal lines of David and Nathan, the priestly lines of Levi and Shimei, and all other clans. Husbands and wives will grieve separately so each person can face God alone. True repentance cannot simply be a public ceremony; it must be an honest, personal sorrow before the Lord.
